[PAPER_0056, relevance_score=0.375] Predictions

Based on the results of Experiment 1 and previous research, we formulated two sets of questions and hypotheses:

1

As a first (although not main) research question, we examined how accent influenced overall processing of words (regardless of language switches). If accent has an influence, we expected RTs on L2-English words to differ between the one-accent and the two-accent tasks. Given that L1-Mandarin words are always produced by an L1-Mandarin speaker, this effect would emerge as an interaction between language (Mandarin vs.

[PAPER_0059, relevance_score=0.350] We also had the following sets of predictions, which went in two different directions, with the second prediction being related to language coactivation and control specifically:

a

If switching between different accents (L1-Mandarin vs. L1-English accents) increases processing time at the phonological level, we expected a significant interaction between trial type (language switch vs. nonswitch) and accent, with a larger switching cost in the two-accent task than in the one-accent task.
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 2 predicted significant switching costs, particularly into Mandarin, and competing effects of accent on switching costs. items.registration_content_quotes: [PREREG_0020, relevance_score=0.322] Finally, Experiment 1 will also allow us to test if the L1 accent during L2 trials in general helps bilinguals process the L2 (due to familiarity with L1 pronunciation) or if, on the contrary, due to heightened interference from the L1 lexicon, it makes such processing more difficult. Thus, we expect to observe a significant Language x Accent interaction (with only English but not Mandarin RTs differing between accent conditions).

The final data set included 97 Mandarin-English bilinguals (65 female, Mage = 27.93, SDage = 7.96) who were tested between July and December 2022. [PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.393] Unfortunately, we could not run simulations with accent and modality as factors, as no previous study had targeted these variables in a set up similar to our study. Note that although we originally planned to collect data from 96 participants only, we received data from 97 eligible participants.

Ninety-four participants were living in the United Kingdom, while the remaining three were not living in the United Kingdom but confirmed they had all previously lived there, which was important as the participants listened to British speakers during the experiment.

[PAPER_0083, relevance_score=0.432] Procedure

The participants completed the study online, within one session of about 30 min. The study was built in Gorilla (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020), and the participants were predominantly recruited via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/) or via SONA (https://www.sona-systems.com/). The testing session comprised the three language switching comprehension tasks (the two tasks of Experiment 2 and the task of Experiment 3, see below), with the task order counterbalanced across participants.

[PAPER_0076, relevance_score=0.383] Design

This study included three within-participants variables: language (English vs. Mandarin), trial type (nonswitch vs. switch trials), and accent (two-accent task with L1-Mandarin words produced by L1-Mandarin speakers and L2-English words by L1-English speakers vs. one-accent task with all words produced by L1-Mandarin speakers).

[PAPER_0088, relevance_score=0.295] The switching ratio differed from Experiment 1, as we wanted to generate similar numbers of trial types across conditions. Category switches (i.e., living vs. nonliving items) were also distributed equally across trial types and language combinations. In all lists, no more than four trials in the same language, of the same type of category or language switch were presented in a row. There was a speaker switch on each trial.

A trial consisted of a 500-ms fixation cross followed by the presentation of the target word.
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 2 varied language, language trial type, and accent within participants. Category switches were also distributed across trial types and language combinations, and response-type switching was included in an exploratory combined-data analysis.
